summary: EU, US, UK, Canadian and many other passports enter Ukraine visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period, and eligible others can use the official eVisa. The UK FCDO says Ukraine's airspace is closed and its borders with Belarus and Russia are closed; its advice covers the crossings with Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, Romania and Moldova.

proofOfFunds.text: Required by law (Article 21 of the Law on the Legal Status of Foreigners). Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 884 of 2013 sets the amount at 20 times Ukraine's monthly subsistence minimum per month of stay, worked out per day as (20 × the monthly minimum ÷ 30) × (days of stay + 5). It can be shown with cash, a bank card with a statement, an accommodation booking, a tour voucher, a host's guarantee letter or a return ticket, and can be checked when a visa is issued and at the border.

payments.text: The UK Foreign Office says ATMs are available and credit cards are widely used in cities, but that because of Russia's invasion ATMs might not be refilled with cash, some bank cards might not be accepted, and ATMs and card terminals may not work during power cuts.

tips.text: The UK Foreign Office says Ukraine's airspace is closed, so entry is overland or by rail through a neighbouring country; check the travel advice for every country you cross.
The UK Foreign Office says to identify shelter locations in advance of any air alert and to take shelter immediately when one is announced; several air raid alert apps exist, including "Air Alert".

The UK FCDO says martial law is in place and to expect more document checks, transport restrictions and curfews, and to carry your passport at all times. Canada's travel advice says to follow local authorities' instructions at all times, including air raid sirens, curfews and evacuation orders.

The UK Foreign Office says Ukrainian and dual-national men aged 23 to 60 are prohibited from leaving Ukraine, and that the authorities may treat you as Ukrainian — for example if you have a Ukrainian parent or were born in Ukraine.
The UK FCDO says your travel insurance could be invalidated if you travel against its advice. Canada's travel advice says to get insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Ukraine?
faq.answer: Citizens of the EU, US, UK, Canada and a broad list of other countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Many other nationalities can apply online for the official eVisa; the rest need a visa from a Ukrainian consulate. Whatever your passport, entry is currently overland only.

faq.question: How do I get to Ukraine if there are no flights?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says Ukraine's airspace is closed, so all entry is by land or rail from a neighbouring country. Check the travel advice for each country you travel through.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Ukraine right now?
faq.answer: No. The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to most of Ukraine, and against all but essential travel to some western regions. It says to identify shelter locations in advance of any air alert, and lists air raid alert apps such as "Air Alert".

faq.question: How does the Ukrainian eVisa work?
faq.answer: Eligible nationalities apply entirely online at evisa.mfa.gov.ua, uploading a passport scan, photo, insurance and supporting documents. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says applications are processed within 1 working day (urgent) or 3 working days; a single-entry eVisa costs USD 20 and allows a stay of up to 30 days.

faq.question: Do Ukraine's martial-law exit restrictions apply to foreign visitors?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says the exit ban applies to Ukrainian and dual-national men aged 23 to 60, and that if you also hold Ukrainian citizenship Ukraine may treat you as Ukrainian — for example if you have a Ukrainian parent or were born in Ukraine.

faq.question: Should I bring cash to Ukraine?
faq.answer: The UK Foreign Office says credit cards are widely used in cities, but ATMs might not be refilled, some bank cards might not be accepted, and card terminals may not work during power cuts — and to make sure you have enough cash in local currency. Canada's travel advice says cash of €10,000 or more must be declared to customs when entering or leaving Ukraine.
